title: Thoreau the pencil maker
hook: Before Walden, Thoreau helped make some of the best pencils in America.
peek: Henry David Thoreau is remembered for a cabin by a pond. For much of his life he also worked in his family's pencil business in Concord, Massachusetts, where his improvements helped Thoreau pencils rival the best imported ones.
lede: Henry David Thoreau's father, John, ran a small pencil-making business in Concord, Massachusetts. American pencils of the time were gritty and greasy next to the fine pencils imported from Europe. Henry joined the family trade as a young man in the late 1830s and set about fixing that, years before he built his cabin at Walden Pond.

bullets.text: Thoreau found that mixing finely ground graphite with clay and baking it gave a smoother, more even lead. A similar method was already known in France, and it is unclear whether he learned of it or worked it out himself.
He also improved how the graphite was ground, so the powder came out finer. Thoreau pencils earned a reputation as among the best made in America, and the family business did well.
In his eulogy for Thoreau, Ralph Waldo Emerson said that once Henry had made a pencil as good as any, he declined to make more, saying he would not do again what he had done once.

In the 1850s the Thoreaus found a better market for their fine graphite: printers used it in electrotyping, a way of copying type. The family moved from pencils towards selling the powder, and Henry kept the business after his father died.
